doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Bus routine on the road and having fun on stage as bandleader
summary: Gibbs describes driving 500 miles between dates as leader and band boy, many sets a night, and his preference for clubs over concerts.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Okay. Did you enjoy being on the road doing the bus routine, visiting city after city, night after night?

You know what, Monk? That part of your life you never thought about because that was part of getting on the bandstand. That led up to getting dressed, showered, changed, whatever. There were some times when we drove 500 miles and I did all the drive — I was the leader, I was the band boy, I used to load up the instruments because I knew we had to place them in the trunk. We had two cars. I had a Cadillac which in those days you could buy it for four thousand, five thousand dollars. And I had what they call a “sedan delivery.” It was like a station wagon without a window. You know? And so then we loaded — I was the band boy, I did all the driving and I had another guy would drive the other car, and sometimes we would drive 500 miles after — we played — Sundays you know we would play the matinee. Those days, believe it or not, we played five or six sets a night. So you’d play at four or five in the afternoon, from three to seven, and then from nine to two or three or four o’clock in the morning you’d play in St. Louis and then like you’d pack up the instruments and get everything ready and go to the hotel check out, boom, everything in the car, drive 500 miles to Toronto, Canada, and maybe get there in time to check in, if not just go right to the job, go change our clothes because we all had, I had uniforms for the band, we all wore dark suits, and get on stage. And once we got on stage Shangri-la came into our lives. We were the happiest idiots you could ever be in your life. But it was the music that meant anything. And to me music has always meant © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

having fun. Me having fun. The audience had fun because we were having fun. You know it’s very infectious. But when I got onstage I always — ‘cause I love clubs. I hate concerts. I hate big — playing at the Playboy Festival was the most money I ever made for a job, but the audience is twenty feet away, the closest person. There’s no rapport with anybody. I get on stage first, and I make sure the band, we have fun. You can talk, you know, you’ve got something stupid, silly, I’m the best straight man you ever had, but don’t fool with the music. Just don’t fool with the music. And I would talk if I saw a bald, heavy guy I asked him, “Do you want a toupee?” I don’t know what I’d say, who knows what I’d say. I became Don Rickles when I was on stage.
